A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same HoT research. Their text, tables, figures, equations, and extensive appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, prompting ablations, model-verification experiments, and a 63-participant human study.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds harder-task evaluations, self-consistency comparisons, hallucination measurements, and attention analysis.

M1.justification: The base HoT procedure, eight-shot prompting, XML tagging, and three-step demonstration construction remain unchanged. Section 5.3 adds an evaluated HoT plus self-consistency variant that samples multiple responses and selects the most frequent answer, providing a limited inference extension.

E1.justification: v3 adds GPQA Diamond and four BBEH tasks: Time Arithmetic, Spatial Reasoning, Shuffle Objects, and Causal Judgement, extending coverage to harder and longer inputs. MultiArith and ASDiv disappear from Table 1 but remain represented in appendix material and the stated 17-task self-consistency evaluation; they are not wholly removed.

E2.justification: v3 Table 6 adds CoT plus self-consistency as a comparator. Repeated Question, already evaluated in v1's ablation, also participates in the broader 17-task comparison. The existing CoT, prompting-ablation, and LLM-verification comparator sets are otherwise retained.

E3.justification: v3 introduces sentence-level SelfCheckGPT evaluation using Gemini-1.5-Pro outputs, four additional responses, and GPT-4o judgments, plus a self-consistency evaluation across 17 tasks using two Gemini models. The new hard-task comparison uses four models. Table 1's arithmetic aggregation changes from seven tasks to five; the retained eight-shot and human-study protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds measurements testing how attention is distributed between facts and XML tokens. Section 5.1 and Appendix R add hallucination diagnostics and paired error examples, while Section 5.3 tests whether HoT's benefits persist with self-consistency. Existing tag-placement, mismatched-tag, small-model, and reasoning-model analyses are largely retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v1 reports benchmark accuracies as point estimates, alongside existing human-study uncertainty values. v3 Table 6 newly reports means and standard deviations over five independent evaluation runs for CoT, Repeated Question, and HoT on two Gemini models across 17 tasks. The self-consistency columns remain point estimates; this does not establish an increase from any particular earlier run count.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial result blocks for hard tasks, hallucination scores, self-consistency, and attention. Table 5 reports mean SelfCheckGPT scores of 21.22 for CoT versus 14.92 for HoT; Table 6 reports 86.22 for CoT plus self-consistency versus 88.79 for HoT plus self-consistency. Retained Table 1 cells, Tables 2–3, and human-study results are unchanged. The arithmetic gain changes from +1.60 to +2.10 because the aggregation excludes two tasks.

T1.justification: The user-verification accuracy equation is retained, moving from v1 Section 5.5 to v3 Appendix C. Neither version introduces substantive formal theory or proofs. The new attention measurements and explanation of SelfCheckGPT are empirical and descriptive.

C1.justification: v1 primarily hypothesizes reduced hallucination and claims accuracy improvements across 17 tasks. v3 explicitly claims reduced hallucination in the abstract and leading contribution, supported by SelfCheckGPT scores, and expands its headline accuracy claim to over 20 tasks. The conclusion emphasizes user-verification speed, although estimated verification-accuracy benefits remain claimed elsewhere.

C2.justification: v3 refines the tentative attention explanation: XML tokens attract attention while enclosed fact tokens receive less, motivating a proposed redistribution away from non-essential tokens. It adds qualifications concerning extremely long inputs, LaTeX/code answers, and medical or multimodal demonstrations. The established small-model failures and human overtrust warning remain.

D1.justification: Appendix O adds missing GSM-Symbolic and Census dataset descriptions and sample counts, and corrects the logical-task descriptions and examples. The new hallucination workflow documents auxiliary sampling, the judge, and XML-tag removal. Existing API versions, temperatures, annotation prompts, visualization code, and code/data access information are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds connections to GUIDE for attention-based motivation, SelfCheckGPT, self-consistency, the new benchmarks, and studies of misleading citations. Some earlier references are removed. Its central positioning—linking response phrases to input facts rather than citing external documents—remains unchanged, as does most related-work coverage.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: contribution statements and method explanations are rewritten or condensed, new evaluations lead the results section, and mismatched-tag analysis, estimated human accuracy, and LLM-verification discussion move into appendices. Appendix organization is extensively revised. The title also changes 'Supportive' to 'Supporting'.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is condensed, Table 1 loses two columns, and multiple existing figures and tables move between the main text and appendices. The compact tag-count/accuracy summary table is removed. v3 adds hard-task, hallucination, self-consistency, and attention tables, plus a SelfCheckGPT workflow diagram and paired hallucination examples; appendix displays are also rearranged.

improvement.justification: The five-run variability reporting and self-consistency comparison strengthen empirical reliability beyond v1, while harder tasks and dedicated hallucination evaluation broaden validation. These gains are tempered by treating a single-model consistency proxy as a hallucination rate and errors in new illustrations: Table T66 labels an HoT answer as without hallucinations despite its contradictory vehicle ordering. The net improvement is positive but limited.
